# Week 5, Day 1.1 - Prerequisites check

Today is about **config files**, so the TypeScript is small: one regular expression literal and
one shallow-copy trap.

| Concept | What it looks like | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| Typed object export | `export default defineConfig({ ... })` | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| Spread with override | `{ ...base, retries: 0 }` | [week3/day5_1](/learn/w3/d5/p1) |
| Array of strings | `testMatch: ["a.spec.ts"]` | [week3/day5_1](/learn/w3/d5/p1) |
| Regex literal | `/@smoke/` | new - below |

**Next:** [Day 1.2 - One suite, two configs](/learn/w5/d1/p2)

## Concept 1 - a regex literal

Slashes instead of quotes. `/@smoke/` is not a string; it is a **pattern object** with a
`.test()` method that answers *does this text contain that?*

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `/@smoke/.test("login @smoke")` | `true` |
| `/@smoke/.test("login @regression")` | `false` |
| `/@smoke/.test("@smoketest")` | `true` - it matches *inside* words too |

That last row is the trap: a tag named `@smoke` also matches `@smoketest`. Keep tag names
distinct.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 2 - combining patterns

`|` means *or*. You will want this the moment you have more than two tags.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 3 - spread copies only the top level

You used spread-with-override in [week3/day5_1](/learn/w3/d5/p1) to build a browser project
out of a preset. Today you build one whole config out of another - which exposes the half that day
did not need: spread is **shallow**. Nested objects are copied as a single value, so naming a
nested key below replaces the whole thing rather than merging into it.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
**Next:** [Day 1.2 - One suite, two configs](/learn/w5/d1/p2)

# Week 5, Day 1.2 - One suite, two configs

Your suite has 400 tests. Before every deploy you want the 40 that matter, in two minutes. Once
a night you want all 400. Same tests, two different runs.

Two things get you there: **a tag in the test title** and **a second config file**.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## Step 1 - tag the tests

A tag is just text in the title. Playwright has no special tag syntax; `@smoke` is a convention
that a pattern can find.

```ts
test("sign in works @smoke", async ({ page }) => { ... });
test("statement export @regression", async ({ page }) => { ... });
```

| Convention | Meaning in practice |
|---|---|
| `@smoke` | fast, run on every commit |
| `@regression` | slow, run nightly |
| `@critical` | must never break; page someone if it does |

The `@` is not required. It just makes the tag easy to spot by eye and unlikely to appear in
prose by accident.

## Step 2 - the spec, and selecting from it

Four tests below: two tagged `@smoke`, two tagged `@regression`.
Four ran. Now select just the fast ones. `--grep` keeps titles that match the pattern.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 3 - `--grep-invert`, the other direction

`--grep` keeps matches. `--grep-invert` throws them away. Useful for *everything except the
slow ones*.

import { runSpec } from "../_shared/deno-helpers.ts";

await runSpec("week5/generated/day1-tagged.spec.ts", { extraArgs: ["--grep-invert", "@regression"] });

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 4 - move the choice into a config file

Typing `--grep @smoke` every time is a thing to forget. Put it in a config and the config
becomes the decision:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  grep: /@smoke/,     // the config selects the tag - no flag needed
  retries: 0,
  workers: 3,
});
```

Two files, one spec:

| | smoke config | regression config |
|---|---|---|
| `grep` | `/@smoke/` | *(none - everything runs)* |
| `retries` | `0` | `1` |
| `workers` | `3` | `2` |
| `trace` | *(default)* | `retain-on-failure` |
| Expected | **2 tests** | **4 tests** |

**2 versus 4, from one spec file.** That is the whole technique.

## Step 5 - what happens when the config and the flag disagree

"The flag overrides the file" is the answer most people give. It is only half right, and the
other half will cost you an afternoon. Run this.

**`Error: No tests found`.**

Not the 2 `@regression` tests. Zero. The CLI `--grep` did **not** replace the config's `grep` -
the two were combined, and a test has to match **both** patterns. No test is tagged `@smoke` *and*
`@regression`, so nothing ran.

`grep` is a **filter**, and filters stack. That is the trap: your config narrows to a lane, and
every `--grep` you type afterwards can only narrow further, never sideways.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

| Setting | Config | Command line | Result | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `grep` | `/@smoke/` | `--grep @regression` | **0 tests** | combined - must match both |
| `workers` | `3` | `--workers=1` | 1 worker | overridden |
| `retries` | `2` | `--retries=0` | 1 attempt, no retry | overridden |

Remember it as: **plain values are overridden; filters are added to.** Every row above was
checked by running it - including the first, which is why this lesson does not say "the flag
always wins".

The practical consequence: to run a different lane, point at a different config. Do not try to
`--grep` your way out of one.

**Next:** [Day 1.3 - How a real repo lays this out](/learn/w5/d1/p3)

# Week 5, Day 1.3 - How a real repo lays this out

Same `grep`, same `testMatch`, same `--grep` - arranged the way a team actually keeps them.

## The layout

```
playwright.config.ts          <- shared settings, the one source of truth
config/
  smoke.config.ts             <- imports the base, overrides 3 things
  regression.config.ts
  ci.config.ts
package.json                  <- names each run so nobody types flags
```

Both lanes kept `baseURL`, and each changed only what it meant to. Drop the `...sharedBase.use`
from `ciLane` and re-run: the second line prints `*** LOST ***`. That one-line difference is the
most common bug in a multi-config repo.

## Where tags come from in a real team

| Who | Adds which tag | Why |
|---|---|---|
| The author of a new test | `@regression` | default; safe, runs nightly |
| Whoever owns the release checklist | promotes a few to `@smoke` | keeps the fast set fast |
| The on-call engineer | `@critical` | this one wakes people up |

The rule that keeps it working: **the smoke set has a time budget.** Two minutes. When it grows
past that, something gets demoted - otherwise `@smoke` slowly becomes `@everything` and the
scheme is pointless.

## Playwright's built-in `tag` option

Newer Playwright takes tags as data rather than title text:

```ts
test("sign in works", { tag: ["@smoke"] }, async ({ page }) => { ... });
```

`--grep @smoke` finds both forms.

| | in the title | `tag:` option |
|---|---|---|
| Survives a title reword | no | **yes** |
| Visible in the report | yes | yes |
| Found by `--grep` | yes | yes |
| What most existing suites use | **yes** | not yet |

Write new tests with `tag:`; expect to read both.

**Next:** [Day 1.4 - Practice](/learn/w5/d1/p4)

# Week 5, Day 1.4 - Practice

No solutions here. Each problem says how to know you got it right.

Work in `week5/generated/`. Copy `day1-tagged.spec.ts` to a new name first so you can always get
back to something that ran.
**Next:** [Day 2.1 - Prerequisites](/learn/w5/d2/p1)

problems.statement:
**A third tag**
Add a fifth test tagged `@critical` to your copy of the spec, then run only it.

**Right when:** `1 passed`, and the smoke run still reports `2 passed`.

**Two tags on one test**
Give one test both `@smoke` and `@critical`. Run `--grep @smoke`, then `--grep @critical`.

**Right when:** that test appears in both runs. Say in one line why no extra config was needed.

**A critical.config.ts**
Write a third config that runs only `@critical`, with `retries: 2` and `workers: 1`.

**Right when:** it runs your critical tests and nothing else, with no flags on the command line.

**Prove the precedence, both halves**
Run your `critical.config.ts` but force `--grep @regression`. Then run it again forcing
`--workers=1`.

**Right when:** the first finds **no tests** and the second runs on one worker - and you can say
in one sentence why the two behave differently.

**An "everything except" run**
Produce a run of every test that is **not** `@regression`, using a config file only - no flags.

**Right when:** the count matches what you predicted *before* running it.

> Hint: `grepInvert` is a config key, the sibling of `grep`.

**Break it on purpose**
Rename a tag to `@smoketest` in one test, leaving `grep: /@smoke/` alone. Predict the count,
then run.

**Right when:** you predicted correctly and can explain it using Day 1.1, concept 1.

**The shallow-spread bug**
Write a config that spreads a base but sets `use: { headless: true }` without spreading
`base.use`, and run a spec that relies on `baseURL`.

**Right when:** it fails on an unresolved URL - the symptom of a lost `baseURL` - and you fix it
with the inner spread.
